newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Leaked paper spurs Jewish outrage at Swiss envoy.
newsitem.headline: Leaked paper spurs Jewish outrage at Swiss envoy.

text.p: Switzerland's strained ties with Jewish organisations worsened on Sunday with publication of a leaked document in which Berne's envoy to Washington called for "waging war" against Jewish groups and other vocal critics.

Swiss Jewish leaders immediately bemoaned the comments, which the SonntagsZeitung weekly said came from a confidential strategy paper ambassador Carlo Jagmetti sent to Berne last month on how to handle a row over dormant accounts in Swiss banks of World War Two Holocaust victims.
"This is a war that Switzerland must wage and win on the foreign and domestic front," said the document, excerpts of which the paper printed. "You cannot trust most of the adversaries," it said.

SonntagsZeitung said the "adversaries" to whom Jagmetti referred were Jewish groups and U.S. Senator Alfonse D'Amato, who have accused the Swiss of profiting cynically from the war and are seeking compensation for Holocaust victims.

The document recommended Switzerland agree to compensation to settle Jewish claims "because Jewish circles and Senator D'Amato must be satisfied quickly" so that "calm will return on all levels", the paper reported.
A foreign ministry spokesman declined comment on the report.
Swiss Jews were shocked by the tone of the document.
"I was shocked to see the insensitivity with which this matter is being addressed," said Thomas Lyssy, vice-president of the Swiss Jewish Federation (SIG).

"When an ambassador in America speaks of "war' and of "domestic and foreign fronts' and of "opponents who are not to be believed', then this shows the significance of this matter is not being recognised.

"Today's report has already shocked the Jewish community in Switzerland. It will also cause an uproar in America. I think this is causing trouble that is completely unnecessary. It is very regrettable," Lyssy said.

The story broke a day after Switzerland's biggest coalition party, the Social Democrats, demanded Economics Minister Jean-Pascal Delamuraz resign for accusing Jewish groups last month of "blackmail" for insisting Berne quickly compensate Jews for wartime suffering.

Delamuraz has since apologised for the remark, made in a newspaper interview as he finished his one-year term in the rotating Swiss presidency, thus heading off threats by Jewish leaders to call a boycott of Swiss banks.
He rejected the call to quit and accused the Social Democrats using the issue to score domestic political points at a time when relations with Jews were slowly starting to improve.

SonntagsZeitung editor Ueli Haldimann wrote in a commentary that Jagmetti's document undermined Swiss efforts to build goodwill by announcing plans for government and big business to open a Holocaust memorial fund.

"This is oil on the fire for all those who contend Switzerland is not acting honestly," he wrote, adding it torpedoed the government's pledge to review unconditionally Switzerland's wartime role and make amends as warranted.
"The Federal Council (cabinet) must make clear that its intent to build bridges is serious...The Federal Council must act quickly, before it is forced to do so by external pressure," he wrote.
